rv.q: Sheehy’s originality makes an evocative play unmissable.
The other actors are uniformly superb in a play that is by turns, convulsively funny, bleak and puzzling.

A year after her Olivier-nominated performance in Machinal, Sheehy’s transformative, vanity and cliche-free turn here underscores how damn good she is and hopefully permanently elevates her to leading-actor status.
McPherson himself skillfully directs a splendid ensemble from which two names have to be singled out.
The real magic here comes from the beautifully woven speeches McPherson gives his characters as they rebel against tedium, death, and the heavens.
I’m not sure it quite adds up, but it’s far more interesting than plenty of plays that do.

In the programme notes for THE BRIGHTENING AIR, playwright director Conor McPherson compares theatre to a pagan church. “…like a religious service, theatre is a distillation of the baffling privilege of being alive.
It is a production that envelops you in the warmth and melancholy of rural Ireland, delivering a family drama that is as evocative as it is quietly magical.
It’s a frustrating play, always watchable, so nearly great, so nearly soaring, yet somehow held earthbound by the weight of its intent.
I can't say I was as moved by Air as I had hoped I might be, given McPherson'
There’s a good, tight three-handed play in there, but the problems arise as the narrative expands beyond that not quite ménage à trois.
McPherson’s writing is as solid as his tenure would have you expect, and there are some genuine compelling threads at play, though none ever seems to be plucked with the focus they ought to.

It points to the basic premise being too convoluted, and regrettably, 150 minutes later, I gained little understanding of the character arcs, or exactly what’s meant to be dramatic about a family nattering over sandwiches. At this point, I should mention that as a deaf critic, the Irish accent is one of the hardest accents for me to understand.
